title: Languedoc, Roussillon and the south
subtitle: France's Mediterranean arc
objectives: Explain their shift from bulk to quality
Name Provence and the south-west's key wines

steps.title: A huge area
steps.body: Languedoc-Roussillon, along the Mediterranean, has about a third of France's vineyards. Once a source of cheap table wine, it now makes characterful blends from Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Carignan and Cinsault. Hot, dry summers and poor schist and limestone soils suit them. Appellations include Faugères, Saint-Chinian, Pic Saint-Loup and Corbières.

steps.title: From bulk to quality
steps.body: Since the 1980s, growers pulled out high-yielding vines, planted better grapes and restored old Carignan. The IGP Pays d'Oc lets producers make varietal wines, like Chardonnay or Merlot, with fewer rules, a big export success. Roussillon is known for its vins doux naturels, such as Banyuls, Maury and Rivesaltes.
steps.highlight: Better grapes, old vines, flexible IGP

steps.prompt: What is IGP Pays d'Oc known for?
steps.explanation: Pays d'Oc allows producers to label and sell wines by grape, with fewer restrictions than the AOPs.

steps.title: Provence and the south-west
steps.body: Provence is the world's reference for pale, dry rosé, mostly from Grenache, Cinsault and Syrah; Bandol makes powerful Mourvèdre reds. The south-west is varied: Cahors for Malbec, Madiran for Tannat, Jurançon for sweet and dry whites, and Bergerac next door to Bordeaux.

steps.prompt: Match each appellation to its grape.
steps.explanation: The south of France is a patchwork of local grapes.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Languedoc-Roussillon is France's largest vineyard area
It moved from bulk to quality, with IGP Pays d'Oc for varietals
Provence leads rosé; the south-west has Cahors, Madiran and Jurançon
